figures.label: Figure 1
figures.caption: The method, drawn from its own artifacts rather than as a schematic. Offline preparation. Patch features of $15{,}000$ captioned COCO images are clustered into $K=640$ visual words, and each term signature is counted from them. The table is the factor $S$ of Equation (1), one row per term and one column per word. Red means a word covers more of an image when captions mention the term and blue less, in multiples of what shuffled captions produce. Per-image inference. One forward pass assigns each patch of a new image to its nearest word on the encoder’s $14\times 14$ grid, by the rule of Equation (2) that described the corpus. That word map is $\Phi$, and scoring a term at a patch reads the row of the term in $S$ at the word of the patch, the product $S\Phi$ entry by entry. The table holds five terms, the row shows the three the image contains, and the three maps share one color scale.
figures.headline: Patches of a new image read the table row of each term at their visual word, so one lookup scores each patch.
citing_sentences: An offline stage builds a table from a caption corpus, and an online stage answers queries about a new image from that table (Figure 1).

figures.label: Figure 2
figures.caption: The permutation null and the ceiling on COCO, drawn with one vocabulary and the hard assignment. (a) The permutation null of Equation (4) for a common term and a rare one, where $\pi$ is the fraction of captions that name a term. “Person”, with $\pi=0.465$, reaches $0.631$ against a null of $0.060$. “Handbag”, named in $34$ of $15{,}000$ captions, with $\pi=0.002$, reaches $3.57$ against $1.85$. On the raw scale the rare term is more than five times larger. Measured in multiples of its own null, however, it is the weaker of the two, at $1.9$ times its null against $10.5$ for “person”. (b) The largest raw signature of every term, its null and the ceiling of Equation (5). Both rise as a term becomes rare, and no term exceeds $0.84$ of its ceiling.
figures.headline: Measured against its own null, the rare term 'handbag' scores weaker than 'person', at 1.9 times its null against 10.5.
citing_sentences: A term whose own $\max_{k}|s_{t}[k]|$ exceeds $\sigma_{t}$ is bound more strongly than chance reaches on nineteen draws out of twenty, and we say it clears its null (Figure 2a).

figures.label: Figure S1
figures.caption: Two further steps of the method on COCO, from one vocabulary of the reported table. (a) The contrast Equation (3) counts, for “cat” and the word its signature is largest on: the share of each image in that word, for images whose captions name “cat” and for the rest, with each group’s mean marked. Images whose captions name “cat” give that word a mean share of $0.071$, against $0.00006$ for the rest. (b) Why the score of Equation (15) blends two estimates. A joint word combines one word from each of the four vocabularies. The bars count joint words by the number of captioned images that contain them, and the red curve is the trust weight $\gamma_{\ell}$ at $\lambda=3$. Of the $178{,}828$ joint words, $83\%$ appear in three images or fewer, where $\gamma_{\ell}$ is at most one half. Most patches therefore rely mainly on the better-supported average of the four vocabularies, and only frequent joint words are trusted on their own.
figures.headline: Joint words combine one word per vocabulary, and 83% of them appear in three images or fewer, so most patches rely on the average.
citing_sentences: With $\lambda=3$, chosen for natural images, a joint word seen once gets weight $0.25$ and one seen thirty times $0.91$ (Figure S1, Section S2 of the supplement).

abstract: Grounding a text query in an image needs a matrix scoring every term against every patch. Vision-language models compute it with an aligned text encoder, which many image encoders, such as histopathology-related models trained on slides alone, lack. The Caption-Anchored Patch-Term Occurrence Representation (CAPTOR) estimates the matrix without a text encoder. It clusters a frozen image encoder’s patch tokens into visual words and describes each captioned image by its share of patches in each word. A term signature is the standardized difference of those shares between images whose captions mention the term and the rest. The matrix factorizes into a term-by-word table and a query-independent image factor, so an image is encoded once and a new term adds one table row. Against every training-free baseline, CAPTOR leads on Common Objects in Context (COCO), Pascal Visual Object Classes (VOC) and Cityscapes. On COCO, scored on the cells one object owns, it reaches $0.565$ mean intersection over union (mIoU) against $0.502$. On all three, it is also level with a text alignment trained on the same backbone, which needs gradients, a text encoder and several times the captions. On held-out breast-cancer slides, it exceeds the strongest baseline scoring patches with a pathology text encoder by $0.160$ mIoU. Read through CAPTOR, UNI, an encoder trained on slides alone, exceeds such baselines by $0.132$ on a common grid. Counting can therefore give a text interface to any image encoder trained without language, wherever captioned images exist.

sections.body: Vision-language models score each term against each patch through a text encoder, and many image encoders, including several histopathology encoders trained on slides alone, have none. CAPTOR builds the same term-by-patch matrix without one. It clusters a frozen encoder's patch tokens into $K$ visual words, describes each captioned image by its share of patches in each word, and scores a term by how those shares differ between images whose captions mention it and images that do not. Against training-free baselines it leads on COCO, VOC and Cityscapes, and it is level with Talk2DINO, a trained alignment, on the same backbone. Stated limits are that Talk2DINO scores higher on COCO and VOC in its released settings, and that CAPTOR uses captions alone while CLIP's text encoder is trained on $400$ million image–caption pairs.
sections.heading: Introduction
sections.headline: Counting caption words over frozen image patches can build a text-query matrix without any text encoder.

sections.body: Table 1 groups earlier methods by what they need. Methods that form the query with a text encoder include CLIP-based dense scoring, ProxyCLIP, which reads two backbones, and Talk2DINO, which maps text embeddings onto DINOv2 features. Trained routes such as Zoom-shot learn a mapping into a text-aligned space and need paired data and gradients. The closest predecessors are caption-counting models from automatic image annotation. Mori et al. counted word-region co-occurrence, and later work fitted expectation-maximization translation models. CAPTOR shares their caption supervision and differs in its standardized contrast, its permutation null, its use of modern foundation patch tokens, its factorized table and its reweighting. The comparison of statistics on shared visual words is deferred to Section 5.1.
sections.heading: Related work
sections.headline: Existing grounding methods read a text encoder or train an alignment, while caption-counting predecessors share only the supervision.

sections.body: CAPTOR splits the term-by-patch matrix into two factors: a term-by-word table and a word map that assigns each patch to one visual word. The words are k-means centroids of the patch tokens of $N$ captioned images, fitted once and held fixed. Each image is summarized by its volume vector, the share of its patches in each word. A term's signature is the difference between mean volumes of images whose captions mention the term and of the rest, in units of each word's standard deviation across the corpus. Each signature is then divided by a permutation null, the 95th percentile of maxima over 200 caption shuffles. Dividing by the null leaves each term's patch ranking unchanged, but it raises COCO mIoU from 0.429 to 0.511 by putting terms on a comparable scale. Pathology gains little, since its terms are all frequent. No gradient is taken.
sections.heading: Method
sections.headline: CAPTOR factorizes the compatibility matrix into a term-by-word table and a per-image word map, with no gradient.

sections.body: The CAPTOR table is counted from captions of a COCO training subset that contains no evaluation image. Evaluation uses the COCO validation images, the VOC validation set, COCO-Object and Cityscapes. In pathology the table is counted from PathCap figures whose captions mention one of $28$ tissue terms, and it is evaluated on BCSS and LUAD-HistoSeg. The matched protocol scores a $14\times 14$ grid over the center crop and keeps only cells that one class covers by more than half. The standard protocol scores every pixel with each baseline's released settings. Each dataset is split into a development half, which chooses settings, and a reporting half, scored once. For BCSS, $41$ of the $103$ patients form the development half and $62$ are scored once. Differences use paired percentile bootstraps over images or patients, and the p-values are not corrected for multiple comparisons.
sections.heading: Experimental setup
sections.headline: The table is counted from captions alone, and every reported number is measured once on a held-out reporting half.

sections.body: On COCO under the matched protocol, CAPTOR reaches 0.565 mIoU against 0.502 for ProxyCLIP given the same propagation, a paired difference of +0.064 with an interval from +0.044 to +0.081. Against Talk2DINO, mIoU is level at -0.001, with an interval containing zero, while CAPTOR is ahead on accuracy by +0.011. CAPTOR is the more precise method, with 0.683 of its assigned patches correct against 0.646, and Talk2DINO the more complete one, recovering 0.810 of patches against 0.740. On the standard protocols CAPTOR reaches 0.559 on Cityscapes and is level with Talk2DINO as released. Its main loss is to objects that captions mention together, such as microwave cells labeled oven.
sections.heading: Results
sections.headline: On COCO, CAPTOR reaches 0.565 mIoU, leading training-free baselines and level with trained Talk2DINO on mIoU.

sections.body: The vocabulary holds only terms that captions mention often enough to clear their nulls, so surfaces and materials, which captions rarely name, lie outside the method. Binding also inherits the level of detail of the captions, as lung stroma shows. An object photographed in one setting can absorb the words of that setting, which is where CAPTOR loses on COCO-Object. Attributes, relations and negation were not tested. Under the hard assignment, patches that share a word are identical for every term. Soft assignment, propagation and joint words relax this, and averaging vocabularies fitted with different seeds removes most of the dependence on one partition. Captions and development labels still supervise the method, and so do the text encoders the baselines read.
sections.heading: Discussion
sections.headline: CAPTOR's vocabulary is limited to terms captions name often, and patches sharing a visual word cannot be separated.

sections.body: CAPTOR estimates the term-by-patch matrix from captions over the visual words of a frozen encoder, without gradients or a text encoder. On natural images it leads the training-free baselines on COCO, VOC and Cityscapes, and it is level there with a text alignment trained on the same backbone. In pathology it gives a text interface to encoders that have none. Through it, UNI, trained on slides alone, names breast tissue better than dense scoring with a trained pathology text encoder. The conclusion is that grounding text in images does not require a text encoder, only captioned images and counting. The authors suggest this opens specialized domains where aligned text encoders and dense annotations are costly to obtain.
sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.headline: Counting over captioned images can ground text in image encoders that have no text encoder.
